title: Should Your Nonprofit Combine Donor and Volunteer Management Software?
summary: Considering one CRM for donors and volunteers? Learn what to compare, how to weigh costs, and what to expect when moving your nonprofit’s data.
body_markdown:
Your volunteer manager knows who shows up every Saturday. Your development team knows who gives every December. Figuring out who does both may mean exporting lists and comparing names.


We hear about this in conversations with nonprofit teams at Giveffect. Their tools still serve a purpose, but staff spend too much time piecing the information together. Development wants a fuller picture of each supporter. The volunteer manager wants to keep the scheduling and registration processes the team worked hard to establish. Leadership needs to understand whether switching is worth the investment.


**We recommend starting with the work your teams need to do together. Then ask whether a shared platform would make that work easier while supporting the processes each department depends on.**


## When should you combine donor and volunteer management?


Combining donor and volunteer management software makes sense when separate systems create duplicate work, leave gaps in supporter histories, or make reporting harder—and a shared platform can address those problems within your budget and staff capacity.


Start with a question your team struggles to answer today:


- Which volunteers also donated this year?
- Which corporate partners supported us through employee volunteering and financial gifts?
- Who attended an event, volunteered afterward, and has stayed involved?
- Can development see someone’s volunteer history before reaching out?


If answering requires several exports and a colleague’s help, bring that example into your software conversations.


## Look at the work between your systems


A donation platform may process gifts well. A volunteer tool may handle scheduling well. The extra work often happens between them.


Someone exports volunteer records so development can identify existing donors. Communications checks an event list against the CRM. A staff member updates an email address, then has to remember where else it appears.


These tasks become part of the routine. When it is time to compare software, it is easy to count subscriptions and overlook the hours spent keeping everything aligned.


Ask colleagues to walk through a recent example. How did they move the information? Who checked it? What happened when two records disagreed?


That gives you something concrete to discuss with a vendor. You can show how the task works today and ask them to walk through how your team would handle it in the new system.


## Protect the volunteer processes your team has built


During a conversation with our team, a volunteer manager brought up a concern many nonprofit teams will recognize. Volunteers had recently been asked to renew their waivers. Would switching platforms mean asking them to register and complete forms again so soon?


That question deserves time in the conversation. Anyone who manages volunteers knows how much effort goes into getting people registered, helping them recover accounts, and making sure they arrive prepared.


Before a demo, ask your volunteer manager which parts of the current process work well and what they would like to make easier.


Everyday task What to ask the vendor to show


Registering a group A coordinator reserves spaces, then each participant submits the required information.


Welcoming returning volunteers Someone registers again, and staff can find their existing history.


Managing applications and waivers Staff can see what is complete, what needs renewing, and who needs a reminder.


Offering shifts to qualified volunteers The right people can find and register for shifts that require particular experience or credentials.


Preparing for a shift Staff can find attendance counts and other details collected during registration.


Handling cancellations The team can update participation and let the right people know.


Also think about how people find places to volunteer with your organization. If a community partner lists your volunteer shifts on its website or shares them through your current platform, ask how people would find and register for those shifts after a switch.


When you meet with Giveffect, bring your forms, registration examples, and questions. We can walk through how your team would handle them and explain which features and package you would need.


## Follow one supporter through the demo


A useful demo should show how the work moves from one person or department to another.


Ask the vendor to follow a supporter through a familiar sequence:


1. They register for a volunteer shift.
2. They complete an application or waiver.
3. Staff record their attendance.
4. They later donate or attend an event.
5. A colleague opens their record and prepares a follow-up.


Then ask to see a report of everyone who both volunteered and donated during a particular period.


Include the situations your staff regularly handle. Someone uses a different email address. A group coordinator reserves spaces before knowing every participant’s name. A volunteer cancels at the last minute.


Seeing those steps helps you understand what daily work will feel like after the switch.


Giveffect connects donor and volunteer management with fundraising, events, email marketing, and reporting. Walking through your own examples helps you see how those capabilities could work together for your organization.


### Make follow-up reflect the whole relationship


A first-time donor may have volunteered for years. A regular donor may have brought colleagues to a service day. Knowing that history can change how you thank someone and who follows up.


A shared record puts more of that context within reach. Your team can recognize the time someone has given alongside their financial support and make the next conversation more personal.


Volunteer service deserves appreciation in its own right. Any invitation to give should reflect the person’s interests and the relationship they have with your organization.


## Work out whether the investment makes sense


**Consolidation may reduce overlapping subscriptions and administrative work. Whether it saves money depends on which tools you can retire and the full cost of the new platform.**


If your current setup includes free tools or inexpensive subscriptions, a broader platform may cost more. Leadership will need to understand what your team would gain, which manual tasks could become easier, and whether those improvements justify the expense.


Use your own costs and examples in the comparison.


Cost to review Questions to answer


Current subscriptions What do we pay for donor management, volunteering, events, email, forms, and related tools?


Staff time How much time goes into moving data, correcting records, and preparing reports?


New platform What is included, and what requires an additional fee?


Getting started What will migration, onboarding, training, and preparation involve?


Software you would keep Which tools will we continue paying for?


Overlapping contracts Have we already renewed systems we hope to replace?


Future costs What will we pay after introductory pricing ends, and as records or users grow?


If you’re working through the budget with leadership, TechSoup’s[guide to planning your nonprofit’s technology spending](https://blog.techsoup.org/en-us/posts/how-should-my-nonprofit-use-its-tech-budget-4-things-to-consider) offers additional questions to consider as you weigh the investment.


Renewal dates are easy to miss when different people manage different tools. In conversations with our team, nonprofits have discovered that systems they hoped to replace had recently renewed. That can affect both the budget and the timing of a move.


When you talk with Giveffect, share how many supporter records you have, who needs access, and what you want to make easier. We can walk through the features and support your team would need and put together pricing around that. Bring a few tasks that take too much time today, so you can weigh the investment against specific improvements in your day-to-day work.


Our[Nonprofit CRM Evaluation Guide and Decision Scorecard](https://www.giveffect.com/nonprofit-resource-center/how-to-evaluate-nonprofit-crm/) can help your team work through those questions.


## Moving your data can feel like the biggest hurdle


Even when your team is ready for better software, moving years of records can give you pause. There are donor relationships, volunteer histories, recurring gifts, and details your colleagues rely on every day. You may also be wondering who will find time to prepare everything while donations still need processing and volunteer shifts still need filling.


We hear those concerns in conversations with nonprofit teams. They deserve clear answers before you commit to a change.


Ask the provider to walk you through the migration process using your own systems and records. What will their team handle? What will they need from you? How will you check that the information arrived accurately? Who will help if something doesn’t transfer as expected?


When you speak with Giveffect, ask us to explain the migration support included in your proposal, your team’s responsibilities, and what needs to happen before you agree on a launch date. Working through those details together can make the project easier to understand and plan around.


You can also use this stage to decide which history your staff need in the new system. Could development recognize a longtime donor? Could the volunteer manager check past participation? Could leadership compare results across years? Those answers help you decide what to move, what to archive, and how staff will find older information.


Before moving forward, confirm:


- How donor and volunteer records for the same person will be matched.
- What happens when records contain different contact details.
- Which activity history, notes, and relationships can transfer.
- Whether volunteers will need to create accounts or complete forms again.
- What is required to move recurring gifts.


For recurring gifts, confirm the process with both the current payment provider and the new platform. Find out what can transfer and whether donors will need to take action.


Giveffect’s[Data Migration Guide](https://www.giveffect.com/nonprofit-resource-center/nonprofit-crm-data-migration-checklist/) can help you prepare.


### What Reconciliation Services experienced


Reconciliation Services had nearly 15 years of records across five systems. Someone could place an order through its catering program, volunteer, and donate, while staff in different departments could miss those connections.


The transition became more demanding when two of the three people originally expected to help lead the migration left the organization, leaving much of the responsibility with Mike Marcus, Community Engagement and Insights Manager.


Mike worked with a dedicated Giveffect migration specialist to review data, map fields, and resolve issues. Recurring donations and historical supporter information were migrated without requiring supporters to take additional action.


He described the support this way:


> “The Giveffect team has been incredibly hands-on.”


The case study was published while the team was still completing implementation. It offers a concrete example of the help a nonprofit received while bringing years of supporter history together.[Read the Reconciliation Services case study](https://www.giveffect.com/nonprofit-resource-center/nonprofit-crm-migration-reconciliation-services/) .


## Find a timeline that works for your people


Development may want a new system ready before event registration opens. The volunteer team may need more time because it just introduced a new application process. Finance may be working around renewal dates.


Put those dates on the table early.


Ask whether moving in stages would make sense and what that would involve. While both systems are in use, staff need to know where to enter information, which system to use for reports, and when they can stop using the old tools.


Include the people who will do the work. They need time to prepare records, learn the system, and try the tasks they will depend on.


Ask about help after launch, too. Some questions only come up when someone is preparing a real report or registering a real group of volunteers. Find out who your staff can turn to when that happens.


## Common questions about combining donor and volunteer software


### Can one CRM manage donors and volunteers?


Yes. Giveffect includes donor and volunteer management within its all-in-one nonprofit platform. Ask how the proposed package would support your scheduling, fundraising, communications, and reporting needs.


### What if our current volunteer software works well?


Write down what your team values about it, including any connections to community partners. Bring those examples to the demo and ask how each process would work after a change.


### Will consolidation reduce our software costs?


It may, depending on the tools you can retire and the new platform’s total cost. Include migration, training, software you would keep, overlapping contracts, and ongoing pricing in your comparison.


### Will we need to move everything at once?


That depends on the systems involved and the plan you agree on with your provider. Ask whether moving in stages is practical and how staff would keep information accurate along the way.


### Will recurring donors need to sign up again?


The answer depends on the payment providers and migration options involved. Confirm the process with both providers before communicating with donors.


## Bring us a task you would like to make easier


Perhaps it is identifying supporters who give and volunteer, preparing a leadership report, or coordinating follow-up after an event.


Bring that example to a conversation with Giveffect. We’ll explore which tools you could replace, how the platform could support your team’s work, and what you would need to plan for a transition.
